screens.title: Event-Driven Programming with Blueprints
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how Unreal Engine's Blueprints respond to events instead of polling for state. Event-driven programming lets your game logic sit idle until something meaningful happens, which keeps execution efficient and your graphs readable. We will study core built-in events like Event BeginPlay and Event Tick, explore collision events for interactions, build Custom Events to encapsulate behavior, and use Event Dispatchers so Blueprints can broadcast messages without tight coupling. You'll also practice debugging event flow with print statements and breakpoints so you can see exactly when nodes execute. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design modular actors that announce state changes, listen for relevant messages, and avoid common pitfalls like overusing Event Tick. For example, you will build a simple Light and LightSwitch pair where the switch broadcasts a toggle and the light binds a handler to turn on or off. That hands-on example demonstrates real benefits of dispatchers: reusability and decoupling. As you work through this chapter, notice where you can trade constant updates for event triggers to improve performance and maintainability.

screens.title: What is Event-Driven Programming?
screens.narratorSegment: Event-driven programming is a model where the flow of logic is determined by discrete occurrences — player input, collisions, timers, or messages — rather than continuous polling. In games, that means actors listen for signals and execute only when those signals occur. This reduces unnecessary work and keeps graphs organized. A concrete example: instead of every frame checking whether a player entered a trigger, use an overlap event that fires once when the player enters. That single event triggers pickup logic, inventory updates, and sound effects. One useful mental model is thinking of actors as radio receivers: they tune into frequencies they care about and only react when a matching broadcast arrives. A common misconception is thinking events replace all control flow; in reality, events complement procedures and timers. Use events for reactive behavior and functions for deterministic operations you call directly. Another mistake is hiding too much logic inside a single event node; prefer breaking behavior into Custom Events so each action is readable and testable. Takeaway: event-driven design keeps runtime work bounded and behavior modular. How could you refactor an existing Tick-heavy actor into an event-driven form?

keyIdea.title: Definition

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is Event-Driven Programming?
Event-driven model
Actors wait for events and then run logic. This conserves CPU and simplifies graphs.
Radio receiver analogy
Actors tune into messages and react only when the right broadcast happens.
Concrete example
Use OnComponentBeginOverlap to trigger a pickup instead of checking positions on Tick.
Common mistake
Putting all logic on Event Tick causes wasteful per-frame computation.
Breakdown
  • Event: a signal that something happened, like BeginPlay, Tick, or an overlap.
  • Listener: a node or event in a Blueprint that executes when the signal arrives.
  • Dispatcher: a broadcaster that sends messages to multiple listeners without knowing them.
Key Takeaway

Prefer events for reactive, rare, or user-driven behavior. Use Tick sparingly for smooth continuous changes.

screens.title: BeginPlay — Initialize with certainty
screens.narratorSegment: Event BeginPlay fires exactly once when an Actor is spawned or when play begins. Use it for initial setup tasks: setting default variables, spawning child actors, registering to dispatchers, or enabling input. For example, a door actor can set its initial state to closed and determine which key is required in BeginPlay. If your actor needs a reference to another actor in the level to bind to its dispatcher, BeginPlay is a common place to acquire that reference and call Bind Event. One subtlety: BeginPlay can fire when an actor is spawned dynamically at runtime, so logic there must assume runtime context and not only editor placement. A common misconception is to put startup logic in the actor's construction script; that script runs in the editor for placement and again in a different context, whereas BeginPlay represents actual runtime start and is the reliable spot for gameplay initialization. When acquiring references, prefer exposing variables and assigning them in the editor where possible; Get All Actors Of Class works for learning or many instances but is less efficient for single references in production. Takeaway: BeginPlay is your dependable runtime initializer — use it to set state and bind listeners for events you expect during play.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › BeginPlay — Initialize with certainty
When to use BeginPlay
Initialize variables, bind dispatchers, and perform runtime-only setup.
Example: Door setup
Set state to closed, determine key requirements, and expose a reference for external binders.
Reference acquisition
Prefer exposing a variable for editor assignment; Get All Actors Of Class is acceptable for demos but less efficient.
Checklist
  • Set initial component and variable states you rely on at runtime.
  • Bind to Event Dispatchers so listeners are ready when broadcasters fire.
  • Avoid editor-only initialization that should run only during play.
Key Takeaway

BeginPlay is the right place for runtime bindings and one-time setup. Use editor variables for direct references when possible.

screens.title: Event Tick — When continuous updates are appropriate
screens.narratorSegment: Event Tick executes every frame and provides Delta Seconds to make frame-rate-independent updates. Use Tick for continuous behaviors that truly need per-frame updates: smooth position interpolation, real-time camera updates, or responsive UI animations. For example, moving a projectile or rotating a fan blade smoothly often uses Tick along with Delta Seconds multiplied by speed to ensure consistent motion across frame rates. However, Tick can be expensive if abused. Running expensive checks, searching large arrays, or performing logic that rarely changes will waste C P U each frame. A common beginner mistake is putting pickup detection on Tick rather than using an overlap event; that causes redundant computation. Alternatives include timers for periodic updates, collision or overlap events for state changes, and custom events triggered by input or other actors. Also consider enabling Tick only when needed: actors can enable or disable Tick at runtime, turning it off when idle. Misconception check: Tick does not guarantee precise timing for long-running sequences — timers or timeline nodes are better for scheduled actions. Takeaway: use Tick for true continuous updates, but favor event-driven triggers and timers to keep performance healthy.

keyIdea.text: Reserve Tick for continuous, per-frame updates. Use events or timers when updates can be event-driven or periodic to save performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Event Tick — When continuous updates are appropriate
Tick essentials
Fires every frame. Use Delta Seconds for consistent motion across varying frame rates.
Appropriate uses
  • Smooth interpolation of position or rotation.
  • Real-time input processing that requires per-frame response.
  • Continuous physics adjustments not handled by engine physics directly.
Alternatives & pitfalls
  • Use OnComponentBeginOverlap for pickups instead of checking distances every frame.
  • Use timers for periodic checks rather than Tick when high frequency is unnecessary.
  • Disable Tick when the actor is idle to save CPU cycles.
Mini Example
// Pseudocode for Tick-based movement
CurrentLocation += Direction * Speed * DeltaSeconds;
SetActorLocation(CurrentLocation);
Key Takeaway

Tick is powerful but costly. Prefer targeted events, timers, or enabling Tick only when necessary.

screens.title: Collision Events — Overlap and Hit
screens.narratorSegment: Collision events are how actors notice physical interactions in the world. OnComponentBeginOverlap fires when another component enters a trigger volume and is ideal for pickups, area triggers, or proximity checks. Event Hit fires on physics impacts and is suited for collisions that depend on impulse or contact information. A typical pickup flow uses a collision sphere with OnComponentBeginOverlap: when the player overlaps, check the Other Actor is the player, call a Custom Event like AddToInventory, play a sound, and destroy the pickup actor. To create the overlap event: select the collision component, go to the Details panel, and add OnComponentBeginOverlap — a node appears in your Event Graph ready to connect. Important checks include verifying the Other Actor type by casting and ensuring collision presets allow overlap events. Misconceptions: overlap and hit are not interchangeable — overlap ignores physics impulses and simply reports proximity, while hit gives contact normals and impact data. Use the right event for your gameplay needs. Finally, use Print String while testing to confirm events fire, and remove noisy prints in final builds. How will you decide between overlap and hit for a given interaction?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Collision Events — Overlap and Hit
Overlap example: pickup
Use a Sphere Collision with OnComponentBeginOverlap to detect players entering pickup range.
Typical flow
  1. Overlap fires when player enters sphere.
  2. Cast Other Actor to PlayerCharacter to confirm.
  3. Call Custom Event AddToInventory and then Destroy Actor.
Hit example: physics impact
Event Hit provides impulse, normal, and hit location useful for effects and damage calculations.
Checks & tips
  • Ensure collision presets allow the event type (Overlap vs Block).
  • Use Print String while iterating to confirm Other Actor values during testing.
  • Use Hit data for realistic responses like bounce direction or damage from impulse.
Key Takeaway

Choose overlap for proximity triggers and hit for physics-based collisions. Test with prints to ensure events fire as expected.

screens.title: Custom Events — Encapsulate behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Custom Events let you package a named sequence of Blueprint nodes into a callable unit. Instead of repeating the same chain multiple times, create a Custom Event like TakeDamage or OpenDoor and call it from different places. You can add input parameters to pass values such as damage amount or a toggle boolean. For example, a TakeDamage custom event might accept a float Amount and reduce health then play a hit animation. Creating a Custom Event is done by right-clicking in the Event Graph and selecting Add Custom Event. A common benefit is clearer debugging: you can place Print String nodes inside the custom event to confirm when that behavior runs, independent of who called it. One misconception is to use Custom Events for everything — they are great for modularity but do not replace functions for pure computations or nodes that must return values. Use Custom Events for procedural sequences and side effects, and functions for deterministic value-returning operations. Takeaway: Custom Events improve reuse and readability; name them descriptively and use parameters to keep interfaces clean. Custom Events — Encapsulate behavior means use custom events to group reusable behavior and pass parameters, keeping blueprint graphs modular and easier to read.. In practical terms, create named events with parameters to keep graphs readable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Custom Events — Encapsulate behavior
Why use Custom Events?
They reduce duplication and clarify intent by giving a name and optional parameters to sequences of nodes.
Create & use
  1. Right-click in Event Graph → Add Custom Event.
  2. Name it descriptively and add input parameters as needed.
  3. Call it from other nodes when you want that behavior to run.
Concrete example
A ToggleLight event accepts a Boolean bOn. When called it sets the Point Light intensity to 5000 if true or 0 if false. This single event can be invoked from a dispatcher binding, a debug button, or other scripts.
Pro Tip
Place prints inside the custom event to confirm when any caller triggers it, making cross-Blueprint debugging easier.
Key Takeaway

Name and parameterize custom events to centralize behavior and simplify caller logic.

screens.title: Event Dispatchers — Broadcast without coupling
screens.narratorSegment: Event Dispatchers let one Blueprint broadcast a message and many other Blueprints bind handlers to react. This pattern avoids tight coupling that comes from direct casting or direct function calls. Think of the dispatcher as a public radio station: the broadcaster announces a message and any subscribed listener responds. To create one, add an Event Dispatcher in the My Blueprint panel and give it a descriptive name like OnSwitchToggled; add parameters if you need to pass data such as a Boolean state. When the broadcaster wants to send the message, drag the dispatcher into the graph and choose Call. On the listener side, get a reference to the broadcaster, then use Bind Event to hook a local Custom Event to the dispatcher — commonly done in BeginPlay so bindings exist before gameplay begins. This architecture enables a switch to trigger multiple effects: open doors, play sounds, and toggle lights without the switch knowing about individual actors. A common mistake is binding repeatedly or forgetting to unbind when necessary in dynamic scenarios; ensure bindings are set once or cleaned up when actors are destroyed. Takeaway: dispatchers give you flexible, decoupled communication — design clear dispatcher interfaces and bind listeners responsibly.

keyIdea.text: Use Event Dispatchers to broadcast state changes or signals so any listener can bind and react without the broadcaster knowing concrete listeners.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Event Dispatchers — Broadcast without coupling
Dispatcher pattern
Broadcaster defines dispatcher; listeners bind to it and receive calls when it's invoked.
Creation steps
  1. Add Event Dispatcher in My Blueprint and name it.
  2. Add parameters to pass data if needed.
  3. Call the dispatcher where appropriate to broadcast.
Binding on another Blueprint
Obtain a reference to the broadcaster, call Bind Event to register a Custom Event, usually during BeginPlay.
Design note
Use descriptive dispatcher names and parameter types so listeners can easily consume the broadcast without guessing what data is sent.
Key Takeaway

Event Dispatchers allow many listeners to react to a single broadcast while keeping the broadcaster ignorant of who listens.

screens.title: Hands-On: Create BP_Light (Light Blueprint)
screens.narratorSegment: In the hands-on activity you first create BP_Light: an actor with a Static Mesh and a Point Light child. Start by adding a Point Light component and set its initial intensity to zero so the light is off by default. Then add a Custom Event named ToggleLight that takes a Boolean input bOn. Inside ToggleLight, use a Set Intensity node to set the Point Light to 5000 when bOn is true and to 0 when false. This isolates the light behavior so any other Blueprint can call ToggleLight or bind to it through a dispatcher. A key benefit of putting this logic in a Custom Event is reusability: whether a switch, a timed event, or a script wants to control the light, they call the same event. A common stumbling point is forgetting to expose the Point Light reference properly; confirm the Set Intensity points to the correct component. After implementing ToggleLight, add a Print String inside the event to confirm runtime calls during testing. This practice makes it straightforward to observe when the light receives toggle requests and helps you verify bindings later when you create the switch.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hands-on: Create BP_Light
Components to add
  • Add a Static Mesh to represent the fixture.
  • Add a Point Light as a child and set Intensity to 0.
  • Expose the Point Light if you need to set it in the editor.
Custom Event: ToggleLight
Create ToggleLight with input bOn (Boolean). Inside: Set Intensity to 5000 if true, 0 if false.
Testing tips
Add a Print String inside ToggleLight to confirm calls during Play. Confirm the Light component reference is correct on the Set Intensity node.
Mini Code Panel
Custom Event ToggleLight(bOn : bool)
  if bOn
    PointLight.SetIntensity(5000)
  else
    PointLight.SetIntensity(0)
  PrintString("ToggleLight called: " + (bOn ? "On" : "Off"))
Key Takeaway

Isolate behavior in a Custom Event so the light can be controlled by many systems without duplication.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how Unreal Engine's Blueprints respond to events instead of polling for state. Event-driven programming lets your game logic sit idle until something meaningful happens, which keeps execution efficient and your graphs readable. We will study core built-in events like Event BeginPlay and Event Tick, explore collision events for interactions, build Custom Events to encapsulate behavior, and use Event Dispatchers so Blueprints can broadcast messages without tight coupling. You'll also practice debugging event flow with print statements and breakpoints so you can see exactly when nodes execute. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design modular actors that announce state changes, listen for relevant messages, and avoid common pitfalls like overusing Event Tick. For example, you will build a simple Light and LightSwitch pair where the switch broadcasts a toggle and the light binds a handler to turn on or off. That hands-on example demonstrates real benefits of dispatchers: reusability and decoupling. As you work through this chapter, notice where you can trade constant updates for event triggers to improve performance and maintainability.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the event-driven model used by Blueprints, identify and use common built-in events, create Custom Events to modularize logic, and implement Event Dispatchers for decoupled communication. You will also know how to debug event flow using print messages and breakpoints so you can verify when events run and inspect values. Each objective builds toward practical skills: recognizing when to use BeginPlay versus Tick, wiring overlap or hit events for interactions, encapsulating repeated behaviors in a Custom Event, and broadcasting a dispatcher so multiple actors can react independently. For example, you will use a switch that calls an Event Dispatcher to toggle lights; the light binds to that dispatcher and runs its own toggle logic. Understanding these objectives matters because well-structured event logic keeps gameplay responsive while avoiding performance costs and tight coupling. A common misconception is that everything must be updated every frame; instead, prefer targeted events and timers. Practice each objective in the hands-on activity to reinforce how events flow in a running game.

This guided objectives view frames how you will practice each skill and how to verify success. First, explain event-driven programming by describing why Blueprints listen for occurrences instead of polling. A good verification is to show an actor that remains idle until an overlap fires. Second, identify and use built-in events: place Print String nodes on BeginPlay and Tick to see firing patterns, then change Tick logic to a timer to compare performance. Third, create Custom Events to hold repeated logic such as toggling a light or applying damage; call that event from multiple places to show reuse. Fourth, implement Event Dispatchers in a Switch actor and bind handlers in a Light actor; your verification step is binding at BeginPlay and toggling in-game to observe the light changing without direct casting. When debugging, use Print String messages and set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables. A common misconception is that dispatchers replace all references; they only decouple callers and listeners and still require a way for listeners to obtain a reference to the broadcaster to bind at runtime.

Event-driven programming is a model where the flow of logic is determined by discrete occurrences — player input, collisions, timers, or messages — rather than continuous polling. In games, that means actors listen for signals and execute only when those signals occur. This reduces unnecessary work and keeps graphs organized. A concrete example: instead of every frame checking whether a player entered a trigger, use an overlap event that fires once when the player enters. That single event triggers pickup logic, inventory updates, and sound effects. One useful mental model is thinking of actors as radio receivers: they tune into frequencies they care about and only react when a matching broadcast arrives. A common misconception is thinking events replace all control flow; in reality, events complement procedures and timers. Use events for reactive behavior and functions for deterministic operations you call directly. Another mistake is hiding too much logic inside a single event node; prefer breaking behavior into Custom Events so each action is readable and testable. Takeaway: event-driven design keeps runtime work bounded and behavior modular. How could you refactor an existing Tick-heavy actor into an event-driven form?

Event BeginPlay fires exactly once when an Actor is spawned or when play begins. Use it for initial setup tasks: setting default variables, spawning child actors, registering to dispatchers, or enabling input. For example, a door actor can set its initial state to closed and determine which key is required in BeginPlay. If your actor needs a reference to another actor in the level to bind to its dispatcher, BeginPlay is a common place to acquire that reference and call Bind Event. One subtlety: BeginPlay can fire when an actor is spawned dynamically at runtime, so logic there must assume runtime context and not only editor placement. A common misconception is to put startup logic in the actor's construction script; that script runs in the editor for placement and again in a different context, whereas BeginPlay represents actual runtime start and is the reliable spot for gameplay initialization. When acquiring references, prefer exposing variables and assigning them in the editor where possible; Get All Actors Of Class works for learning or many instances but is less efficient for single references in production. Takeaway: BeginPlay is your dependable runtime initializer — use it to set state and bind listeners for events you expect during play.

Event Tick executes every frame and provides Delta Seconds to make frame-rate-independent updates. Use Tick for continuous behaviors that truly need per-frame updates: smooth position interpolation, real-time camera updates, or responsive UI animations. For example, moving a projectile or rotating a fan blade smoothly often uses Tick along with Delta Seconds multiplied by speed to ensure consistent motion across frame rates. However, Tick can be expensive if abused. Running expensive checks, searching large arrays, or performing logic that rarely changes will waste C P U each frame. A common beginner mistake is putting pickup detection on Tick rather than using an overlap event; that causes redundant computation. Alternatives include timers for periodic updates, collision or overlap events for state changes, and custom events triggered by input or other actors. Also consider enabling Tick only when needed: actors can enable or disable Tick at runtime, turning it off when idle. Misconception check: Tick does not guarantee precise timing for long-running sequences — timers or timeline nodes are better for scheduled actions. Takeaway: use Tick for true continuous updates, but favor event-driven triggers and timers to keep performance healthy.

Collision events are how actors notice physical interactions in the world. OnComponentBeginOverlap fires when another component enters a trigger volume and is ideal for pickups, area triggers, or proximity checks. Event Hit fires on physics impacts and is suited for collisions that depend on impulse or contact information. A typical pickup flow uses a collision sphere with OnComponentBeginOverlap: when the player overlaps, check the Other Actor is the player, call a Custom Event like AddToInventory, play a sound, and destroy the pickup actor. To create the overlap event: select the collision component, go to the Details panel, and add OnComponentBeginOverlap — a node appears in your Event Graph ready to connect. Important checks include verifying the Other Actor type by casting and ensuring collision presets allow overlap events. Misconceptions: overlap and hit are not interchangeable — overlap ignores physics impulses and simply reports proximity, while hit gives contact normals and impact data. Use the right event for your gameplay needs. Finally, use Print String while testing to confirm events fire, and remove noisy prints in final builds. How will you decide between overlap and hit for a given interaction?

Custom Events let you package a named sequence of Blueprint nodes into a callable unit. Instead of repeating the same chain multiple times, create a Custom Event like TakeDamage or OpenDoor and call it from different places. You can add input parameters to pass values such as damage amount or a toggle boolean. For example, a TakeDamage custom event might accept a float Amount and reduce health then play a hit animation. Creating a Custom Event is done by right-clicking in the Event Graph and selecting Add Custom Event. A common benefit is clearer debugging: you can place Print String nodes inside the custom event to confirm when that behavior runs, independent of who called it. One misconception is to use Custom Events for everything — they are great for modularity but do not replace functions for pure computations or nodes that must return values. Use Custom Events for procedural sequences and side effects, and functions for deterministic value-returning operations. Takeaway: Custom Events improve reuse and readability; name them descriptively and use parameters to keep interfaces clean. Custom Events — Encapsulate behavior means use custom events to group reusable behavior and pass parameters, keeping blueprint graphs modular and easier to read.. In practical terms, create named events with parameters to keep graphs readable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Event Dispatchers let one Blueprint broadcast a message and many other Blueprints bind handlers to react. This pattern avoids tight coupling that comes from direct casting or direct function calls. Think of the dispatcher as a public radio station: the broadcaster announces a message and any subscribed listener responds. To create one, add an Event Dispatcher in the My Blueprint panel and give it a descriptive name like OnSwitchToggled; add parameters if you need to pass data such as a Boolean state. When the broadcaster wants to send the message, drag the dispatcher into the graph and choose Call. On the listener side, get a reference to the broadcaster, then use Bind Event to hook a local Custom Event to the dispatcher — commonly done in BeginPlay so bindings exist before gameplay begins. This architecture enables a switch to trigger multiple effects: open doors, play sounds, and toggle lights without the switch knowing about individual actors. A common mistake is binding repeatedly or forgetting to unbind when necessary in dynamic scenarios; ensure bindings are set once or cleaned up when actors are destroyed. Takeaway: dispatchers give you flexible, decoupled communication — design clear dispatcher interfaces and bind listeners responsibly.

In the hands-on activity you first create BP_Light: an actor with a Static Mesh and a Point Light child. Start by adding a Point Light component and set its initial intensity to zero so the light is off by default. Then add a Custom Event named ToggleLight that takes a Boolean input bOn. Inside ToggleLight, use a Set Intensity node to set the Point Light to 5000 when bOn is true and to 0 when false. This isolates the light behavior so any other Blueprint can call ToggleLight or bind to it through a dispatcher. A key benefit of putting this logic in a Custom Event is reusability: whether a switch, a timed event, or a script wants to control the light, they call the same event. A common stumbling point is forgetting to expose the Point Light reference properly; confirm the Set Intensity points to the correct component. After implementing ToggleLight, add a Print String inside the event to confirm runtime calls during testing. This practice makes it straightforward to observe when the light receives toggle requests and helps you verify bindings later when you create the switch.

Next, implement BP_LightSwitch. Add a Static Mesh for the switch and a Box Collision component slightly larger to detect the player. In My Blueprint add an Event Dispatcher named OnSwitchToggled with a Boolean parameter bIsOn. In the Event Graph, use OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentEndOverlap on the Box Collision to detect the player entering and leaving; on begin overlap call the dispatcher with bIsOn true, and on end overlap call it with false. In the BP_Light's BeginPlay, get a reference to the BP_LightSwitch — for learning, you can use Get All Actors Of Class and pick the first result, though exposing a variable and assigning it in the editor is a cleaner production approach. From that switch reference drag and use Bind Event to OnSwitchToggled, creating a local Custom Event named HandleSwitchToggle that receives bIsOn and calls ToggleLight on this BP_Light. Test by playing: walking into the switch's box should toggle the light on, walking out toggles it off. Use Print String in both the dispatcher call and the HandleSwitchToggle to confirm event flow. A common error is forgetting to bind before the dispatcher fires, so bind in BeginPlay to ensure readiness.

Event Tick runs every frame and supplies Delta Seconds for frame-independent motion, but use it only for necessary continuous updates.
